=== Slow is Fast for Filing.pdf ===
This gives Abbott a graceful way to pause 765kV projects on purely technical issues alone, no
politics. The 765kV STEP has no protection from Geomagnetically Induced Current (GIC)
harmonics per SB 6. Author is Don Brown, co-founder Secure the Texas Grid.




Source: https://substack.com/inbox/post/216223743
SECURE THE TEXAS GRID


“Sometimes Slow is Fast”
Harmonics will bring our grid down if we don’t take action. It is only a question of when.
SECURE THE TEXAS GRID
SEP 17, 2026




“Sometimes Slow is Fast”

This is a quote by Steven R Covey, that stays with me, especially with
regard to relationships. Covey’s leadership point is that it is faster to go
slow actively listening and building trust in relationships than a “git her
done” approach that values speed over understanding.

Large projects, like the 765kV transmission lines in Texas, involve many
stakeholders and many complex relationships. At stake is our economy,
our security, and our deep-seeded Texas values. This is a big, Texas-sized
bet and it is worth taking time to get it right.

We have so much going for us as a state, controlling our own grid and
being energy rich. We can move faster than any other state. We can be
quick to address disasters and to mitigate future threats. But that same
ability to move fast can become a liability resulting in misaligned goals
when ignoring key constituents’ concerns.

Most people don’t know that Texas residential and small business rate
payers are paying 178% higher rates than Texas commercial rates. That is
the highest percentage rate difference in the nation! It is also a case of
 misaligned goals created by federally subsidized, now stranded,
renewable wind and solar investments, transmission infrastructure costs
to move that stranded power, long-term commercial power-purchase
contracts to achieve lower cost for big business and a positive ESG score,
and a market model that still doesn’t differentiate between the value of
24-hr dispatchable generation and intermittent renewable generation.
Would you value a car that you can only use 7 hours a day the same as
one that is available 24 hrs a day?

Many of these were a disjointed patchwork of solutions over the last two
plus decades that we continue to learn from. Hindsight is 20/20 and I
am not judging. Missteps are frequently part of being a first-to-market
mover in any industry. Texas laid out the welcome mat for every wind
and solar venture. And now we are putting band aids to stabilize
reliability with battery storage units that can go right next to your
neighbor’s house or your child’s school or over your county’s water
supply. It has been a build, break, fix, regulate cycle. The key is to not
repeat past mistakes particularly where there is no tolerance for error,
that is, for unrecoverable events.

Now it appears again that growth and reliability are being prioritized
over costs, property rights, and grid resilience. Many will argue that this
is where we are today on the 765kV lines that the PUC just approved. The
project scope creeped, much to the legislature’s surprise. Likely due to
the pressure of meeting the super high growth projections emerging in
2024 and 2025. CCN processes were rushed and for 1400 property
owners, not even followed. The PUC then approved the first 2 legs of the
project in opposition to the recommendation made by the Senate
Business and Commerce and the House State Affairs Committees to
pause the project.

There were compelling arguments made on both sides of the decision
during the hearings. But it is hard to slow down growth when so much
money and market share is involved. I did not envy PUC Chair Gleeson
 in making this decision or being responsible for the potential long-term
consequences as a result.

Even so, there are critical resilience issues that were never
addressed by ERCOT, the PUC, or the transmission service
providers. These are issues currently being studied by the
newly formed Grid Security Commission. The good news is
that it is not too late to take these issues into consideration.
But a pause may be justified on technical grounds, and yes,
“Sometimes Slow is Fast”, particularly when it involves the
entire state’s health, safety, and livelihood. Let the
commission do their job.

The reason to state “it is only a question of when” is because we know
from the history of events such as the 1989 Quebec event that it was
harmonics that took down the grid. The 1920 railroad event and the
Carrington event were even larger. Geomagnetic events are happening all
the time. It is simply a matter of when one that is large enough, actually
orders of magnitude higher than the current grid GIC E3 protection
standard used in Texas.

We encourage Chairman Gleeson and Governor Abbott to consider the
following: The 765kV project, as approved has…

1) No protection from GIC harmonics: Harmonics from
geomagnetic induced currents do over $10B annually in damage in the
US according to a 2014 peer-reviewed statistical analysis of more than
11,000 insurance claims for industrial electrical equipment losses in
North America, jointly conducted by Lockheed Martin, Zurich Insurance,
and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and a follow-
on 2015 Zurich, Lockheed-Martin authored economic impact analysis.
Data Centers will surely be concerned to see that a low-cost solution
exists that Texas failed to address.
 2) Risk of total collapse: The simultaneous loss of multiple extra-
high-voltage transformers or other large equipment across the Texas in a
single event could result in a regionwide long-term blackout, during
which the essential services described by Section 44.004, Utilities Code,
including water treatment, health care, financial services, and
communications, would be unable to operate normally. Unlike any other
natural disaster, this is not recoverable. Replacement transformers of the
type used in extra-high-voltage transmission and generation
interconnection service are custom-manufactured, are sourced
predominantly from foreign suppliers, and historically require four to six
years or longer to design, manufacture, and deliver.

3) Texas Utilities designing to an outdated standard: in May
2025, the International Electrotechnical Commission published Edition
2.0 of IEC 61000-2-9, an internationally recognized standard describing
the E3 high-altitude electromagnetic pulse waveform, superseding the
1996 first edition and providing a more technically current basis than
earlier reference materials for designing equipment to withstand GIC
half-cycle saturation of large power transformers and the generation of
harmful harmonics caused by E3 pulses and geomagnetic
disturbances; This standard supports the 85v/km E3 protection
recommendation in SB 75 which passed in 89(R).

4) Potential for transformers becoming harmonics
generators: a generator step-up transformer (GSU) or other large
power transformer that is not equipped to block or mitigate
geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) does not merely risk damage to
itself: unmitigated GIC drives the transformer into half-cycle saturation,
causing it to generate harmful harmonic currents which increase as GIC
magnitude increases, propagate onto the connected transmission and
distribution system, and are further amplified as they travel into lower
voltage which can damage large power generators, high-voltage circuit
breakers, transformers, voltage support equipment and other critical
grid components, as well as equipment owned by ratepayers. The
 damage could extend well beyond the 765kV transmission
lines.

5) Has not considered that the cost for prevention is a tiny
fraction of the total project cost: Texas Public Policy Foundation
estimates the cost of the total project will be over $100B or over $5,000
per average residential rate payer over the life of the project
(40+yrs). Cost for protection would amount to only $13 per average rate
payer over the life of the project or about 1/400th of the cost. In this
cost estimate, we use the same cost modeling that TPPF used with cost of
equipment and installation of a Capacitive Neutral GIC Blocking Device
(NBD) for a single large power transformer of approximately
$650,000. We have reached out to AECT President, Mark Bell to
conduct a cost workshop for the TSPs. This offer still stands.

Please see “The Invisible Current” for an excellent 10-minute
explainer video on the threat and the affordable and validated
solution. This video was recently shared with members of the White
House NSC.

Don Brown

Co-Founder, Secure the Texas Grid



References for Sometimes Slow is Fast


References

   1. Schrijver, C.J., Dobbins, R., Murtagh, W., & Petrinec, S.M. (2014). “Assessing the
      Impact of Space Weather on the Electric Power Grid Based on Insurance Claims
      for Industrial Electrical Equipment.” Space Weather, 12(7), 487–498.
      Peer-reviewed paper – Wiley/AGU
      Analysis of 11,242 insurance claims showing a statistically significant relationship
      between geomagnetic activity and electrical/electronic equipment claims.
 2. NOAA Science Council. “Space Weather Literature Review.”
    NOAA summary of Schrijver et al. research
    Independent federal summary of the 11,242-claim study and its findings.
3. Zurich Insurance Group (2015). “Electrical Claims and Space Weather: Measuring
    the Visible Effects of an Invisible Force.”
    Zurich 2015 report
    Source for the estimated economic impact “on the order of” $10 billion annually in the
    United States, with the report's stated uncertainty.
4. Electric Power Research Institute. “Mitigation of Geomagnetically Induced
    Currents in Transformers.”
    EPRI technical report
    Technical discussion of GIC, transformer half-cycle saturation, harmonic generation,
    reactive-power consumption and transformer impacts.
5. Pulkkinen, A., et al. (2017). “Geomagnetically Induced Currents: Science,
    Engineering, and Applications Readiness.” Space Weather.
    Peer-reviewed Space Weather paper
    Explains transformer half-cycle saturation, harmonic injection and risks to
    protection/control systems.
6. Tousignant, D., Bolduc, L., & Dutil, A. (1996). “A Method for the Indication of
    Power Transformer Saturation.” Electric Power Systems Research, 37(2), 115–120.
    Peer-reviewed transformer saturation paper
    Supports the statement that a saturated transformer acts as a source of harmonic currents.
7. International Electrotechnical Commission. IEC 61000-2-9:2025, Edition 2.0,
    “Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) – Part 2-9: Environment – Description of
    HEMP Environment – Radiated Disturbance.”
    Official IEC standard page
    Published May 14, 2025; replaces the 1996 edition and updates early- and late-time
    HEMP information.
8. Texas Legislature, S.B. 75, 89th Legislature, Regular Session (2025), Enrolled
    Version.
    Official SB 75 enrolled text
    Creates the Texas Grid Security Commission and specifically addresses E1/E3 EMP,
    GMD, EHV transformers and an 85 V/km E3 resilience benchmark.
9. Texas Utilities Code, Chapter 44, Grid Resilience.
    Official Texas Utilities Code Chapter 44
    Establishes the Texas Grid Security Commission and identifies essential infrastructure
    and resilience areas.
10. Texas Public Policy Foundation (2026). “Economic Assessment of the 765-kV
    Transmission Plan.”
    TPPF economic assessment
    Source for TPPF's approximately $33 billion capital-cost estimate and “nearly $100
    billion” estimated lifetime cost.
11. Texas Tribune (Aug. 19, 2026). “Residents and Industry Leaders at Odds Over
    Transmission Lines at Legislative Hearing.”
    Texas Tribune coverage
     Documents the legislative hearings, landowner concerns, 180-day CCN controversy and
    legislative calls to reconsider or halt the 765-kV buildout.
12. Texas Tribune (Aug. 24, 2026). “Texas' Data Center, Transmission Line Pauses
    Could Be Risky.”
    Texas Tribune CCN and legislative coverage
    Documents HB 5066's reduction of the CCN decision period from 365 to 180 days,
    utility-industry acknowledgement of problems with the shortened process, and the letter
    from 30 House members.
13. Utility Dive (2025). “Transformer Supply Bottleneck Threatens Power System
    Stability as Load Grows.”
    Transformer supply-chain report
    Reports transmission-scale transformer lead times of approximately three to six years,
    with specialized units taking longest.
14. Secure the Grid Coalition. “The Invisible Current.”
    The Invisible Current technical presentation and source collection
    Useful as a secondary/advocacy source for the neutral-blocking technology, testing
    history and cost claims. It should not substitute for EPRI, IEC, peer-reviewed literature
    or government sources where those are available.
